sections.overview: The Pacific Swift is a large, dark swift that breeds in eastern and northern Asia and migrates south to Southeast Asia and Australasia. It spends most of its time in fast, sustained flight above cliffs, forests and open country.
sections.identification: Adults usually measure 17–21 cm long, have a 43–54 cm wingspan and weigh about 42–43 g. Japanese measurements for the local subspecies give 17.9–20.5 cm body length, 170–195 mm wing length, 10–13 mm tarsus and 39–56 g mass. Sexes look alike; no sex-specific size difference is reported. The body is dark, with a bright white rump and pale throat, long sickle-shaped wings and a deeply forked tail. White feather edges make the underside look scaled. Compared with the House Swift, Apus nipalensis, it is larger and longer-winged, with a deeper tail fork and clearer pale scalloping below; the House Swift is smaller, shorter-tailed and more uniformly dark underneath.
sections.habitat: It occurs across coastal, forested and open landscapes, nesting mainly in cliff crevices and cavities, sometimes in caves or sheltered building sites. Japanese birds arrive for the summer, while northern and eastern populations migrate south for winter.
sections.diet: It catches flying insects in open air, often circling through swarms. Prey include flies, bees, wasps, termites, beetles and moths.
sections.behavior: Its fast flight alternates shallow wingbeats with glides, and large flocks can form during migration. Long journeys connect Asian breeding areas with tropical wintering grounds, although timing varies among populations.
sections.reproduction: It nests in colonies on cliffs and other rocky surfaces, using ledges, cavities and crevices; some populations also use sheltered parts of buildings. Both adults share nesting duties, but comparable clutch and incubation figures are unavailable across the species’ range.
sections.ecology: As an aerial insectivore, it feeds above land and coastal habitats and depends on abundant flying prey; its migration links distant breeding and wintering ecosystems.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment, amended in 2019 from its 2016 evaluation, classifies the species as Least Concern. In Japan, a government assessment of the local subspecies reports a stable or expanding mapped range but fewer survey records and individuals, and suggests that feeding habitat may be worsening.
